PaperTitle: Quantum Computing in the NISQ
ThesisCitingParagraph: L128: Current quantum processors remain in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era \cite{Preskill2018Quantum}, where the performance of quantum circuits is strongly limited by hardware noise \cite{Arute2019Nature}. In realistic devices, computation is affected by multiple error sources, including fabrication imperfections, decoherence induced by environmental coupling, control errors, crosstalk between qubits, and readout noise \cite{Schoelkopf2008Nature,Krinner2022Nature,Sarovar2020Quantum,Nachman2020npjQI}. As circuit depth increases, these noise sources accumulate rapidly and cause measured outputs to deviate significantly from ideal theoretical predictions \cite{Kandala2019Nature}. This noise problem is one of the main obstacles preventing near-term quantum devices from delivering reliable large-scale practical advantage \cite{Bharti2022RMP,Kim2023NatureUtility}.

PaperTitle: Quantum error correction for quantum memories
ThesisCitingParagraph: L132: At a more fundamental level, quantum error correction (QEC) provides a rigorous framework for protecting quantum information by encoding logical qubits into many physical qubits and actively correcting errors during computation \cite{Terhal2015RMP}. In principle, QEC offers a long-term route toward fault-tolerant quantum computing. However, its implementation requires large hardware overhead, potentially requiring millions of physical qubits to run practical algorithms \cite{Gidney2021Quantum}, as well as frequent syndrome extraction and physical error rates below the fault-tolerant threshold, all of which remain beyond the capability of current NISQ devices.

PaperTitle: Error mitigation with Clifford data regression
ThesisCitingParagraph: L138: A more systematic mitigation strategy is probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) \cite{Endo2018PRX}. In particular, Pauli-twirling-based PEC transforms a general noisy channel into an effective Pauli channel that is easier to analyze and invert \cite{Berg2023NatPhys}. PaperTitle: Error statistics and scalability of quantum error mitigation formulas
ThesisCitingParagraph:
L166: The main advantage of PEC is that it can remove bias rather than merely suppressing it approximately. However, this benefit comes at the cost of increased sampling overhead. The variance of the estimator generally grows with the $L_1$ norm of the quasi-probability coefficients, which means that accurate mitigation may require a large number of circuit samples. This bias-variance trade-off and the associated growth of statistical fluctuation in error-mitigated estimators have been analyzed in Ref.~\cite{Qin2023npjQI}. Consequently, a practical PEC framework must address not only the construction of the inverse channel, but also the management of sampling cost and execution efficiency.

L814: At the same time, the Gaussian distribution of the PEC results is broader than that of the corresponding No-PEC results. This trend is again consistent with the theoretical behavior of probabilistic error cancellation: the quasi-probability reweighting reduces the bias of the noisy estimate and improves the mean CHSH value, but it also amplifies the statistical fluctuation of the mitigated estimator \cite{Qin2023npjQI,Tsubouchi2025npjQI}. This effect is reflected in the larger standard deviations of the PEC results, namely $0.037$ versus $0.029$ for the ibm\_fez case and $0.016$ versus $0.012$ for the ibm\_boston case.

L874: Another common feature is that the Gaussian distribution of the PEC results is broader than that of the corresponding No-PEC results. This behavior is consistent with the theoretical expectation of probabilistic error cancellation \cite{Qin2023npjQI,Tsubouchi2025npjQI}. The quasi-probability reweighting suppresses the bias of the noisy result and moves the mean fidelity toward the ideal value, but it also amplifies the statistical fluctuation of the estimator. Therefore, the PEC results become more accurate in their mean value while also exhibiting a larger variance.

L876: Taken together, these teleportation results demonstrate two important points. In addition, the device-dependent truncation behavior is compatible with the broader practical-QEM picture reported in recent mitigation studies, where noise structure and mitigation overhead jointly determine the final execution cost \cite{Qin2023npjQI,Henao2023npjQI,Liao2024NatMachIntell}. First, the proposed PEC package can effectively improve noisy-circuit results for the teleportation task. Second, the same class-based mitigation workflow remains valid across different IBM-device noisy models, which supports the general applicability of the package rather than a device-specific tuning to a single backend.

PaperTitle: Zero-noise extrapolation for quantum-gate error mitigation with identity insertions
ThesisCitingParagraph: L136: Among existing QEM methods, zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) is one of the most widely used because of its conceptual simplicity and relative ease of implementation. ZNE works by intentionally amplifying circuit noise, for example through gate folding or pulse stretching \cite{He2020PRA, Dumitrescu2018PRL}, and then extrapolating the measured values back to the zero-noise limit \cite{Kim2023Nature}. Although effective in many small-scale demonstrations, ZNE becomes less reliable for deeper circuits, where accumulated noise and finite coherence time lead to large uncertainty in the extrapolation \cite{Takagi2022PRL, Quek2023PRL}. Moreover, because ZNE does not explicitly invert the noise process, its correction capability is limited when the error structure becomes more complicated.

PaperTitle: Practical Quantum Error Mitigation for Near-Future Applications
ThesisCitingParagraph:
L138: A more systematic mitigation strategy is probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) \cite{Endo2018PRX}. In particular, Pauli-twirling-based PEC transforms a general noisy channel into an effective Pauli channel that is easier to analyze and invert \cite{Berg2023NatPhys}. By expressing the inverse noisy process as a quasi-probability expansion over Pauli operations \cite{Berg2023NatPhys}, PEC enables unbiased estimation of ideal expectation values when the underlying noise model is sufficiently accurate. Recent advances such as virtual distillation, Clifford Data Regression (CDR), benchmarking-oriented unified frameworks, and learning-based methods have further expanded this domain \cite{Huggins2021PRX,Czarnik2021Quantum,Bultrini2023Quantum,Strikis2021PRXQ,Kim2020IEEEAccess,Liao2024NatMachIntell}.
